À Saint-Léonard, la sécurité des jeunes: In Saint-Léonard, youth safety and the low political participation of the Maghrebi community are emerging as burning issues ahead of the 2025 municipal elections. I wanted to understand why, in a borough where this community is the majority, it remains so underrepresented in public life.
Au cours de mes rencontres, mères, acteu: In my conversations, mothers, community workers, young people and candidates revealed a complex reality made up of fear, distrust of institutions and a lack of spaces for young people, but also hope for a civic renewal.

<strong>À Saint-Léonard, la sécurité des: In Saint-Léonard, youth safety and the civic participation of the Maghrebi community are emerging as central issues in the 2025 municipal campaign. The community is the majority in the borough but still underrepresented on the political scene, and it faces a double reality: growing worry about the violence affecting its young people, and difficulty making its voice heard in public debate. These elections could well expose the tensions of a borough torn between fear, engagement and a search for recognition.
Langelier, Lacordaire, Jean-Talon Est –: Langelier, Lacordaire, Jean-Talon East – along Saint-Léonard’s main thoroughfares, election posters show the names and faces of the candidates running in the November 2, 2025 municipal election. For the first time in nearly 20 years, the borough will have to choose a new mayor, as Michel Bissonnet has decided to bow out after a long tenure. It seems an ideal moment to renew the political landscape in a neighbourhood undergoing deep demographic change.
Derrière les couleurs partisanes et les: Behind the party colours and campaign slogans, one worry dominates residents’ conversations: the safety of young people. In recent years, the neighbourhood has been shaken by gun violence, and the tragedies that have claimed the lives of several teenagers – including Meriem Boundaoui, Mehdi Moussaoui and Yanis Seghouani – remain open wounds.
La communauté maghrébine compose la plus: The Maghrebi community makes up the largest share of the borough’s population. It numbers more than 20,000 people, most of them of Algerian origin. Yet only three candidates from this community are running among the parties in the race. This timid political representation is compounded by chronically low civic participation. The abstention rate in the 2021 municipal election was in fact over 62%, a phenomenon that the neighbourhood roundtable, among others, has pointed out.
<strong>La peur des parents et l’urgence: Parents’ fear and the urgent need for a tailored dialogue
Parmi les voix citoyennes, celle de Nabi: Among the voices of residents, Nabila Bouchala’s resonates strongly. A Saint-Léonard resident for six years, she knows the worries of Maghrebi families well. A lecturer in UQAM’s Department of Sociology and the mother of a teenage girl, she says she feels the weight of a diffuse threat every day. “There are gangs recruiting, they go all the way to Saint-Exupéry secondary school to attract young people. Before, they recruited 15-year-olds. Now it’s much less than that: it’s 14-, 13-, 12-year-olds!” she exclaims. Parents are very afraid, Ms.<sup> </sup>Bouchala continues, especially since the gangs have also been targeting young girls for some time now.
Ces enjeux n’échappent pas à son regard: These issues don’t escape her sociologist’s eye. Indeed, despite the size of the community, the support and socialization opportunities available to its members are insufficient: “There’s a lack of spaces for expression, where people can recognize themselves in certain forms of expression, of civic participation. There’s a lack of support, in reality.”
De plus, les initiatives, notamment cell: Moreover, initiatives, particularly those taken by the borough and the Quebec government to protect young people and promote integration, will remain ineffective, in her view, as long as the approach stays superficial: “We haven’t tried hard enough to understand the problem from the inside. […] There haven’t really been any studies, any sociological investigations to understand the phenomenon. We have a global view, a meta view of the problem,” laments Nabila Bouchala. Without suitable structures, this void leaves the field open to recruiters, who exploit teenagers’ need to belong, she concludes.
Le problème est aussi renforcé par une p: The problem is also reinforced by deep distrust of institutions. “Elected officials only show up during elections,” Ms.<sup> </sup>Bouchala laments, also citing “a break with the schools” and “constant anxiety around the DPJ” (youth protection services). The DPJ is seen by “many parents [...] as a threat,” who are “afraid it will take their children away.” Without dialogue, she says, these fears feed negative perceptions on both sides: “When the two sides don’t communicate, when there’s no space where everyone can express themselves, it’s clear that people stay stuck in their fantasy about the DPJ,” she says. Then she immediately adds: “And on the other side too, whether it’s elected officials or the schools, they also stay stuck in a negative view – not all of them, but many – a negative view of immigration.”
Pour M<sup>me </sup>Bouchala, le prochai: For Ms.<sup> </sup>Bouchala, the next city council should “make sure to involve parents, to involve the young people who are part of the problem so that they become part of the solution.” To do so, she says, it will need to adopt an approach suited to the particularities of this population, which she notes is marked by a strong oral culture. Future elected officials will therefore need to “prioritize grassroots outreach aimed at building strong ties and strengthening political literacy as well as civic participation.”
<strong>Rétablir la confiance : un défi: Rebuilding trust: a central challenge of the municipal campaign?
Hadjira Belkacem, figure de la communaut: Hadjira Belkacem, a community figure and coordinator of the Association de la sépulture musulmane au Québec, refuses to let youth violence be reduced to Saint-Léonard: “Gangs move around. This scourge exists everywhere in Quebec, even in Canada. But because Saint-Léonard is mostly Maghrebi, the label gets stuck on one community.” In her view, this stigmatization prevents the rift between citizens and institutions from healing. “Politicians, we only see them during election season. […] The resources exist, but they don’t work. […] The same strategies produce the same results,” she says.
Par ailleurs, « beaucoup de familles veu: Moreover, “a lot of families want to leave; it’s become unlivable,” warns Ms.<sup> </sup>Belkacem. Her anger reflects a deep exhaustion: “Here, we have to fight for everything: school, the hospital, the police, the DPJ,” she confides, describing a daily life marked by weariness and made worse by the rise in anti-Muslim rhetoric: “We’re tired. We didn’t come here to fight.”
Membres de la communauté maghrébine de S: Members of the Maghrebi community in Saint-Léonard, Montréal. Photo credit: Édouard Desroches
Qu’elles s’expriment comme mères ou comm: Whether they speak as mothers or as community figures, Ms.<sup> </sup>Bouchala and Ms. Belkacem paint the same picture: a stigmatized community, worried about its youth and distrustful of the institutions meant to protect it. “Between politicians and the reality of ordinary people, there’s a rift,” adds Hadjira Belkacem.
<strong>Grandir sans espace : quand les: Growing up without space: young people look for their place in Saint-Léonard
À 19 ans, Marwa* parle avec calme, mais: At 19, Marwa* speaks calmly, but her words land like a clear-eyed observation: in Saint-Léonard, young people lack places to gather. “There aren’t really any spaces where young people can get together, do activities, or just spend time without hanging out outside,” she explains. Born in Canada to Maghrebi parents, she is a student and goes to the Forum jeunesse de Saint-Michel – in a neighbouring borough – for lack of a similar place in her own. “It’s a shame, but if there were something like that in Saint-Léonard, I’m sure a lot of young people would be interested. It could create momentum, get young people off the street.”
Ce sentiment de vide structurel correspo: This sense of structural emptiness matches the findings of Thi-Thanh-Hiên Pham, Nathalie Boucher and Étienne Perrault-Mandeville in a study titled Être jeunes au bon endroit ? Cartographie critique des espaces négatifs pour les jeunes à Saint-Léonard. The researchers describe a fragmented territory, where some areas are “isolated, poorly served and lacking in public facilities.” These zones, they specify, become true “negative spaces,” that is, places where “isolation reinforces the perception of a blocked future.”
Jeunes de la communauté maghrébine à Sai: Young people from the Maghrebi community in Saint-Léonard, in Little Maghreb. Photo credit: Édouard Desroches
Pour beaucoup d’adolescents, expliquent-: For many teenagers, they explain, the street becomes a substitute for failing institutions: a space of belonging and recognition, even at the risk of going astray.
Les constats du <l1><em>Forum citoyen su: The findings of the Forum citoyen sur la sécurité urbaine, organized in February 2025 by Concertation Saint-Léonard, point in the same direction. Participants – parents, young people, organizations, elected officials, police officers – stressed the urgent need to create “safe and appealing spaces” for young people. Among the six priorities that emerged from the forum are the “creation of socializing spaces for teenagers” and the need to “repair the bond between institutions, schools and families.”
Le témoignage de Mélissa Allache illustr: Mélissa Allache’s testimony concretely illustrates the conclusions and observations of the experts behind these studies and consultations: in Saint-Léonard, the lack of suitable spaces doesn’t just breed boredom, it weakens the sense of belonging and widens the gap between young people and institutions.
<strong>Deux voix pour une communauté en: Two voices for a community seeking representation
À Saint-Léonard, trois candidatures issu: In Saint-Léonard, three candidates from the Maghrebi community stand out: Arij El Korbi (Ensemble Montréal), Abdellah Azzouz (Projet Montréal) and Amina Bahri (Équipe Saint-Léonard).
Première élue d’origine maghrébine à Sai: The first elected official of Maghrebi origin in Saint-Léonard, Arij El Korbi, elected in 2021, is seeking a new term as borough councillor under the Ensemble Montréal banner.
M<sup>me </sup>El Korbi défend une appro: Ms.<sup> </sup>El Korbi advocates an approach centred on prevention and local roots. Her platform proposes, among other things, more partnerships with community organizations for “everything related to developing programs for young people,” and an expansion of the police patrol introduced a few years ago to monitor parks from spring to fall.
Mais au-delà de ces « moyens traditionne: But beyond these “traditional means,” she acknowledges that “what can truly make a difference is opening up community spaces,” because in Saint-Léonard “unfortunately, we have far less municipal space for our residents.” She is counting on the extension of the Blue Line of the metro, slated to open in 2031, to ensure “there will be a community centre and sports fields for young people – spaces they can make their own.”
Face à elle, Abdellah Azzouz incarne une: Facing her, Abdellah Azzouz embodies a new political generation. He arrived in Quebec as a child and has worked as a community outreach worker for several years, and he knows the realities of Saint-Léonard’s youth intimately. “Saint-Léonard wasn’t a poor neighbourhood. It’s becoming one, and infrastructure hasn’t kept up,” he observes. In his view, the absence of suitable places heightens the feeling of exclusion: “We need independent spaces, not tied to school, or home, or a place of worship — places where young people can do what they want, feel valued.” His platform proposes providing lasting support to community organizations through long-term funding, creating independent youth centres and encouraging co-operation among schools, police, parents and outreach workers. “We shouldn’t be looking to point fingers, but to build bridges. Young people want to be heard, and so do their parents,” he sums up.
Quant à Amina Bahri, éducatrice en milie: As for Amina Bahri, a school-based educator for more than twenty years and the mother of a daughter, she is running under the Équipe Saint-Léonard banner. Ms. Bahri highlights her own integration journey and her experience with families in the neighbourhood. Concerned with better social cohesion, she says she wants to “build bridges between the different communities to create just one, strong and prosperous.” In her campaign, public safety and services to residents are at the top of her priorities, along with “listening to needs and simplifying life for families and seniors.”
Malgré la méfiance, la fatigue et les bl: Despite the distrust, the fatigue and the wounds, something seems to be shifting in Saint-Léonard. Young people’s words and residents’ reflections sketch the outline of a community that, little by little, is making its voice heard. It remains to be seen whether the next city council will be able to hear it.
